title: The field of Siffin
hook: Ali's army and Mu'awiyah's meet, Qur'ans are raised on spears, and arbitration is agreed

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Battle of the Camel, and Ammar, who honored Aisha from the other side. Your line was believers against believers.

Spears go up along a battle line, and on their points are not banners but pages. Pages of the Qur'an. The army holding them is Syrian, led by Mu'awiyah, the governor of Syria and a kinsman of Uthman. Facing them is Ali's army. They have fought for days on a plain near the Euphrates, and the histories say Ali's side was pressing hard. Then the pages rise, and a call goes across the field: let the Book of God judge between us.
screen: `SPEARS GO UP.` → `PAGES, NOT BANNERS.` → `LET THE BOOK JUDGE.`

segments.voice: Mu'awiyah had refused to pledge to Ali until Uthman's killers were handed over; Ali held that Mu'awiyah must first accept his caliphate. Neither would move, and the armies met at Siffin. The raised pages, the histories say, were the idea of Amr ibn al-As, on Mu'awiyah's side. A sincere call to the Qur'an, or a way to stop a losing fight? The sources leave room for both readings. Ali, reports say, suspected a stratagem. But soldiers in his own ranks would not fight against the raised pages, and they pressed him to accept. He agreed to arbitration: one man chosen by each side, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari for Ali, Amr ibn al-As for Mu'awiyah, to judge by the Qur'an and the Prophet's way. Bukhari preserves a voice from those days. Sahl ibn Hunayf, who was with Ali, tells his own side: suspect your own opinion. He reminds them of Hudaybiyyah, when the Prophet accepted a truce that looked like a defeat, Umar objected, and the truce turned out to be an opening. A settlement can be right even when it feels like losing. How Muslims judge Siffin differs. In Sunni teaching, Ali was in the right and Mu'awiyah erred in his judgment, while Mu'awiyah is still counted a companion. Shia Muslims see Mu'awiyah as a rebel against the rightful Imam and read the pages as a trick. Either way, the picture stays: pages on the spears, and a battle stopped for words.
screen: `NEITHER WOULD MOVE.` · `AMR'S IDEA, THE HISTORIES SAY.` · `ONE JUDGE FROM EACH SIDE.` · `SUSPECT YOUR OWN OPINION.` · then, large: `PAGES ON THE SPEARS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a standoff where neither side will move first, and notice the voice that says talking now would be losing. Borrow Sahl's words, suspect your own opinion: not dropping it, just holding it more loosely, and picture one small offer to talk. If you pray, you can ask for an open heart in it.
Siffin, the plain near the Euphrates where Ali's army and Mu'awiyah's met, pages of the Qur'an were raised on spears, and arbitration was agreed. Today's word.
Your line: pages on the spears. A text can open talks or close them. Day eight hundred eighty-three, done.

howItsDone: Muslims study Siffin as part of the history of the fitnah; Sunni teaching holds Ali was in the right while counting Mu'awiyah a companion, and Shia Muslims regard Mu'awiyah as a rebel against the rightful Imam.
